untested: Whether coastal sea-salt deposition raises soil sodium and weakens aggregates. No paper matched this wording.

web.text: Coastal soils do show more exchangeable sodium close to the coast, with soils nearest the shore past saline-sodic limits and 1.5-2 km inland not. One Egyptian transect showed no steady trend. No source measured aggregate stability, so the aggregate-weakening step is untested.

why: Strength: coastal soils already show higher exchangeable sodium near the shore and past saline-sodic limits within about 1.5-2 km, and a surf-zone-to-inland transect with turbidity tests is a standard one-season design. Risk: sea spray also delivers Ca, Mg and high electrolyte, which keeps clay flocculated and can offset sodium-driven dispersion (an Egyptian transect showed no steady trend), and groundwater or parent material can mimic the gradient.
title: Sea-salt spray raises coastal soil sodium and weakens aggregates

untested: Whether soil Streptomyces aerosols seed cloud droplets or ice. Four papers matched but all are unrelated (enzyme expression, indoor spore release).

web.text: Raindrops are known to throw soil bacteria into the air, and fungal spores can act as ice nuclei. Nothing found on Streptomyces or geosmin particles acting as cloud nuclei.

why: Strength: rain splash demonstrably throws soil bacteria into the air and fungal spores are modelled as ice nuclei, and the stated rain-simulator plus CCN-counter test is standard. Risk: the chain has three uncertain links (spore lofting, activation as CCN or INP, a density correlation surviving background aerosol), and Streptomyces spores are hydrophobic and rare, so the sign could be flipped by the signal being swamped or absent against sea-salt and dust CCN.
title: Soil Streptomyces aerosols from rain seed cloud droplets

untested: Phage killing of methane-oxidizing bacteria and its effect on methane oxidation.

papers.title: T4-type phages diversity in wetland soils reveals their ubiquity and their likely host-dependent dynamics

web.text: No soil study shows phage lysis lowering methane uptake. A bioreactor report says phage blooms can set back methane oxidizers, supporting the direction. A lake study found phages that carry a methane-oxidation gene, which hints at the opposite effect. Sediment work found viruses infect methanotrophs but their genes do not directly drive methane metabolism.

why: Strength: a bioreactor report shows phage blooms setting back methane oxidizers and lysis killing hosts directly lowers oxidation, with a 13CH4 SIP readout. Risk: 0.02 um filtrate swaps and mitomycin C induction also change nutrients and stress responses, and phage that carry methane-oxidation genes or lysis that recycles nutrients to survivors could flip the sign to no change or higher uptake.
title: Phage lysis lowers methanotroph oxidation in soil

why: Strength: Diffuse light raises canopy photosynthesis in smoke haze, and root respiration follows recent photosynthate within days, so the chain has measured links at both ends. title: Hazy diffuse light raises root-driven soil respiration

Thinning reduces soil carbon dioxide but not methane flux from southwestern USA ponderosa pine forests

title: Fire changes the soil methane sink for years

Green et al. 2022: nitrous oxide sources in soil (did not separate chemical from biological production or test subzero temperatures)

web.text: Takenaka et al. (1992, 1996) found nitrite reactions run about 100,000 times faster in freezing solutions at pH 4.5. Soil buffering and the eutectic cut-off make the direction uncertain.

why: Strength: freeze-concentration speeds nitrite reactions by up to 100,000-fold in freezing solutions at pH 4.5 (Takenaka 1992, 1996), and the sterile versus live 15N-nitrite design at five temperatures can falsify it cleanly. Risk: nobody has shown this in soil, Wertz 2018 saw nitrite accumulate at -2 C, and soil buffering at pH 7 could keep nitrite loss lower than at +1 C because Arrhenius slowing outweighs concentration, and the test is falsified if either pH fails.
title: Freezing speeds the chemical loss of nitrite and nitrous oxide in soil

A paper on the copper chaperone for nitrous oxide reductase: below 0.5 uM copper a mutant strain accumulated up to about 4 mM nitrous oxide (read through a summary, not in full)
A paper describing the copper-sulfur cluster at the nitrous oxide reductase active site (read through a summary, not in full)

title: Sulfate and copper shortage raise nitrous oxide release in wetlands

Bommarco et al. 2012: oilseed rape and pollination, +18% seed weight per plant (repository page; yield and quality only)

title: Sulfide starves methane-makers of nickel and cobalt in peat

11-year follow-up at the same FACE: no significant main effect of O3 or CO2 on soil C; the early O3 reduction in new soil C proved temporary, mirroring fine-root biomass; no urban gradient

why: Strength: the Aspen FACE experiment gave a direct 50% reduction in new soil carbon formation under O3 plus CO2, and the proposed 13C fumigation test is standard. Risk: the 11-year follow-up found no significant O3 main effect and the early reduction proved temporary, and fine-root regrowth or ozone-tolerant genotype shifts could erase it while the NOx scaling remains untested.
title: Ozone halves new soil carbon, but only briefly

untested: Site-level multi-year chamber records along a rainfall gradient regressed on lagged ENSO with soil water as mediator have not been done; the wet-forest sign (less waterlogging raises respiration) is untested and competes with a warming/drought-suppression effect in the wet tropics.

papers.title: Synthesis of East Asian forest soil respiration vs ENSO: positive correlation in tropical-subtropical zones, negative in warm temperate, mediated by monsoon precipitation anomalies; lags of months; database synthesis, not automated chambers or mediation by soil water

Tropical water availability versus CO2 growth-rate coupling became more negative 1989-2018, linked to ENSO teleconnection shifts; used atmospheric CO2 and water storage, did not measure soil respiration or a wet versus dry sign split

web.text: Regional syntheses show ENSO-linked soil respiration responses whose sign depends on climate zone and precipitation anomalies, matching the idea of a wetness-dependent sign. The specific waterlogging mechanism in wet forests is mostly inferred, and tropical El Nino heat and drought usually suppress carbon uptake rather than waterlogging.

links.label: ENSO and forest soil respiration, East Asia 2025

why: Strength: synthesis data already show ENSO-linked soil respiration with a sign that varies by climate zone and precipitation anomaly, and chamber networks along a rainfall gradient exist. Risk: the wet-forest rise from reduced waterlogging is inferred, not measured, and El Nino heat and drought usually suppress tropical forest carbon uptake and soil respiration, so warming-plus-drought suppression in wet forests could flip the predicted sign.
title: El Nino flips soil respiration sign by site wetness

untested: Upscaling to land-surface energy balance and evaporation using crust-cover maps and a land-surface model, and a scraped-versus-intact paired transect across a full successional gradient, are not yet done.

papers.title: Mature scytonemin-rich cyanobacterial biocrust raised surface soil temperature by up to 10 C and lowered albedo; plot scale, did not upscale to energy balance or evaporation

20-year warming experiment: crust shift to lightly pigmented cyanobacteria raised brightness 14% and changed surface temperature ~0.3 C per 10% cover; remote sensing at plot scale, argued the feedback is missing from process models
Warming and altered watering raised dryland biocrust albedo by more than 30% via crust community shifts; field experiment, no energy-balance modelling

web.text: The plot-scale effect (scytonemin crust darkens soil and warms it by several degrees, up to 10 C) is published, and follow-up work shows crust community shifts change albedo and temperature. The global-scale energy-balance and evaporation consequence is flagged as missing from models and remains the open part.

why: Strength: scytonemin-rich crust is already measured to lower albedo and raise surface soil temperature by up to 10 C (Couradeau 2016), so the sign is directly measured at plot scale. Risk: only upscaling to the energy balance and evaporation is open, and crust moisture retention or shading could offset warming, but that affects magnitude more than the albedo and temperature direction.
title: Dark biocrust warms dryland surface by several degrees

untested: No study found adding Bdellovibrio or Myxococcus to AOB cultures or ammonium-amended soil and tracking amoA and nitrite; whether AOB flocs protect them from predators, and any ammonium dependence, is untested.

papers.title: Protozoan predation on AOB and anammox in nitritation-anammox biofilms by FISH-CLSM; showed predation of AOB occurs, but by amoebae, not predatory bacteria, and no nitrification rates
Review of Bdellovibrio-and-like organisms as biocontrol agents: prey range is broad Gram-negative bacteria; no data on nitrifier prey or nitrification effects

web.text: Predation on AOB is documented for protozoa and phages, and BALOs have broad Gram-negative prey ranges, so the mechanism is plausible. I found no direct test on nitrifiers, and aggregated, slow-growing nitrifier flocs may be poorly accessible to predators.

why: Strength: Bdellovibrio has broad Gram-negative prey ranges and AOB (Nitrosomonas, Nitrosospira) are Gram-negative, and a culture plus soil experiment with amoA and nitrite readouts is simple. Risk: AOB grow in dense flocs and biofilms that protect them from predators, and slow-growing prey may be too few to sustain predators, so soil nitrification could be unchanged, and the high-ammonium dependence adds a second uncertain link.
title: Predatory bacteria may cut ammonia-oxidiser nitrification

untested: A controlled phage-enriched versus virus-reduced microcosm design with 18O-water CUE and amino-sugar markers is not found; existing results show the sign of the viral effect on CUE depends on soil fertility, opposite to the stated prediction in rich soils.

papers.title: Virus particle addition to agricultural soils raised microbial CUE and necromass by 14% in organically fertilized soil, but raised CO2 by 41% in unfertilized soil; contradicts the prediction in rich soils, supports it in poor soils
Long-term microplastic field experiment: viral lysis and virus-host coadaptation altered CUE and SOC accrual; correlative, not a manipulated virus-reduced design

web.text: Recent work directly manipulates soil viruses and finds both effects: virus addition boosted CUE and necromass in nutrient-rich soils but raised respiration in poor soils. The prediction of uniformly lower CUE with lysis is therefore too simple.

why: Strength: The microcosm design with 18O-water CUE and necromass markers is standard and can be run in weeks. Risk: a 2026 manipulation raised CUE and necromass by 14% with virus addition in fertilized soil, the opposite of the prediction, and lysis recycles carbon to survivors, so the viral shunt can raise CUE in rich soils.
title: Soil viral lysis lowers microbial carbon use efficiency

untested: A controlled spectral measurement of paired soils along an organic carbon gradient at fixed moisture, with albedo forcing compared directly to CO2 forcing from the carbon change across soil types and climates, is not found; existing work is cropland modelling or two-site field trials.

papers.title: European cover-crop modelling with a soil darkening feedback scenario: higher SOC darkens soil and could erase ~20% of the climate benefit; model-based, not measured spectral albedo along a SOC gradient

Zimbabwe maize trials (EGU abstract): albedo forcing and SOC forcing were similar in size and opposite in sign on light sandy soil with mulch, but cooling on dark clay; two sites, two seasons, conference abstract

web.text: Soil darkening with organic matter is long known and recent studies quantify albedo forcing against SOC forcing, finding offsets from about 20% in Europe-wide modelling up to near-total offset on light sandy soil. The result depends strongly on soil type, snow and cover, so a general offset is not established.

why: Strength: soil darkening with organic matter is long known, a European model and Zimbabwe field data both show albedo forcing offsetting 20% to near-all of SOC forcing, and a fixed-moisture spectral gradient is a standard lab measurement. Risk: published work already quantifies much of this so little is new, and real-world cover, snow and moisture can hide bare-soil albedo, though a competing mechanism large enough to reverse the sign is not apparent.
title: Carbon-rich dark soil offsets part of climate benefit

untested: Global or multi-biome test of sign by soil moisture regime using SRDB or flux towers with ENSO lags, and its contribution to CO2 growth-rate variability, is not done; most evidence is regional or atmospheric.

papers.title: Synthesis of East Asian forest soil respiration vs ENSO: sign differs between tropical-subtropical (positive) and warm temperate (negative) zones, heterotrophic more sensitive, driven by monsoon precipitation; regional only
Tropical water availability coupling to atmospheric CO2 growth rate, ENSO teleconnections; showed water control of the growth rate but did not separate soil respiration from photosynthesis

web.text: ENSO is known to drive interannual CO2 growth variability and a regional soil respiration synthesis finds opposite-sign responses by zone. Attribution of the growth-rate signal to soil respiration versus gross primary production and fire is unresolved.

links.label: ENSO and forest soil respiration, East Asia 2025

why: Strength: a 2025 East Asia synthesis already shows positive responses in tropical and negative in warm temperate zones, matching the predicted sign split by moisture regime. Risk: SRDB records are sparse and mostly annual so ENSO lags are hard to resolve, and the claim that soil respiration adds to CO2 growth variability can flip sign because photosynthesis and fire dominate the tropical signal and may offset respiration changes.
title: El Nino shifts soil respiration by region

untested: No study found that separates transpiration-driven drying from other plant effects on gross nitrification (planted versus unplanted or shaded pots at controlled evaporative demand with 15N pool dilution and amoA); plant ammonium uptake and nitrification-inhibitor exudates are confounding mechanisms.

papers.title: Planted versus unplanted forest soil under constant moisture or drying-rewetting: plant ammonium uptake halved by drying while microbial uptake rose; short 24 h assay, nitrification not measured

Shrubland soil incubation with 15N pool dilution across moisture and temperature: gross nitrification rose with water content and ceased below ~60% WHC; unplanted soil, no plant or transpiration effect

web.text: Nitrification is well known to depend on soil moisture with a mid-range optimum, and plants compete with nitrifiers for ammonium. Whether transpiration demand sets a moisture-driven nitrification peak, distinct from direct ammonium competition, has not been tested.

why: Strength: nitrification has a well-known mid-range moisture optimum, with gross rates rising with water content and ceasing below about 60% WHC, so a planted-versus-shaded pot design with 15N pool dilution is workable. Risk: separating transpiration drying from plant ammonium uptake needs tight control, and plant ammonium competition and root nitrification inhibitors could lower nitrification in planted pots regardless of moisture, reversing or masking the predicted direction.
title: Plant transpiration drying shapes soil nitrification rates

untested: No field thaw-depth warming experiment with faunal exclusion (mesh bags or heat extraction) measuring CO2, CH4 and litter mass loss was found; the depth-range expansion of fauna into thawed layers and the effect beyond temperature alone are untested.

papers.title: Lab incubation of Yedoma permafrost with the springtail Folsomia candida for 25 days: CO2 rose ~26%, about half from springtail respiration and ~13% attributed to priming; single species, bacteria only, no field or depth test
Five years of open-top-chamber warming in permafrost wetlands (Great Hing'an Mountains): Collembola richness and abundance rose, about eightfold in April; no decomposition or carbon flux measured
Mini-review of arthropod responses to Arctic cryosphere decline including permafrost depth; highlights data gaps on functional roles

web.text: Warming increases springtail abundance in permafrost wetlands, and adding springtails to permafrost raised CO2 beyond their own respiration in the lab. What is missing is a field test with faunal exclusion that shows the effect on thawed-carbon loss and depth colonization.

why: Strength: a 25-day Yedoma incubation showed springtails raising CO2 about 26% with about 13% attributed to priming, and warming plots raised Collembola abundance about eightfold in April. Risk: springtails are surface dwellers that may not reach deep thawed carbon and mesofauna grazing can cut fungal biomass, and fauna respiration may be a small share of flux, so net acceleration beyond temperature could be near zero or negative.
title: Springtails and mites speed thawed permafrost carbon loss

untested: Isotope tracing (33P or 15N) of nutrient delivery through hyphae to plants across snow-manipulation plots, and the generality beyond one subalpine meadow and AMF, are not shown; the preprint infers nutrient effects from soil pools. It also is not peer reviewed.

papers.title: Preprint: experimentally advanced snowmelt in a subalpine meadow caused plant greening to start early and cut extraradical AM hyphal production, with smaller available N and P pools; one site, not yet peer reviewed, nutrient transfer not traced

Hubbard Brook 29-month root-exclusion and ingrowth cores along a snow-depth gradient: grouped AM and EM abundance unaffected by snow depth, ericoid fungi rose with snow, some orders responded; single sampling, no hyphal timing or nutrient transfer

web.text: A recent early-snowmelt experiment reports plant-fungal asynchrony with reduced hyphal production and smaller nutrient pools, which closely matches the prediction. A forest snowpack-decline study found little change in grouped mycorrhizal abundance, so the effect may vary by system and fungal group.

why: Strength: a 2025 preprint of advanced snowmelt in a subalpine meadow found early greening, reduced extraradical hyphal production and smaller N and P pools, matching the prediction. Risk: it is one site and not peer reviewed, nutrient transfer was not traced, and Hubbard Brook found no snow-depth effect on grouped AM and EM abundance, and soil freeze damage or earlier fungal activity under warmer soil could offset or reverse the nutrient effect.
title: Thin snow causes fungus-plant mismatch and lower nutrient delivery

untested: Multi-year (3-5 year) persistence of the abundance-up, richness-down shift and its link to measured C and N turnover (CUE, N mineralisation) has not been shown; follow-ups were 7 months or less, and the copiotroph shift was inferred from taxa rather than traits or rates.

papers.title: Hurricane Otto, Costa Rica: soil sampled 3 months before and 7 months after; microbial biomass up, genus richness down, shift to dominant functional-group genera; single storm, short horizon, no turnover rates

Luquillo Canopy Trimming Experiment: green debris deposition and canopy opening decoupled; soil microbial community changed pre vs post but did not separate by treatment, effects possibly missed or masked; bacterial richness showed a positive response to some treatment

web.text: A Costa Rica study found the predicted abundance increase and richness decrease after a hurricane, but the best controlled experiment (Luquillo canopy trimming) found treatment effects were masked by strong background variation and resilience. Multi-year persistence and process-rate consequences remain unmeasured.

why: Strength: Hurricane Otto soil showed microbial biomass up and richness down seven months on, and canopy trimming plots already exist as a manipulation platform. Risk: the Luquillo experiment found treatment effects masked by background variation and resilience, so persistence for 3-5 years and a measurable turnover change are uncertain, and community recovery within a year or two would flip the long-term sign.
title: Hurricane litter boosts microbes, cuts diversity for years

untested: No test with trees in seasonally dry forest or shrubland that measures protease activity and gross N mineralization with lift blocked by trenching or shading and deuterium-labelled deep water; existing work is sagebrush with augmented deep water and grass in pots, with no protease assays.

papers.title: Sagebrush field experiment: adding deep water raised lift, soil respiration and 15N cycling in surface soil and N uptake into inflorescences; shrub not tree, no protease assay or blocked-lift control
Grass in two-layer pots with lift blocked by 24 h light: decomposition and uptake higher with lift, mixed NH4/NO3 signs; greenhouse, grass, no protease or gross mineralization by pool dilution
Hydraulic redistribution may stimulate decomposition: diel drying-rewetting of root litter in a desert system; decomposition only, not enzymes or N rates

web.text: Field and pot experiments show hydraulic lift raises topsoil decomposition and N cycling in sagebrush and grass. The specific claim for trees, protease activity and gross mineralization with a blocked-lift contrast, and the 20-100% size, are untested.

links.label: Hydraulic lift and N cycling in grass, 2012

why: Strength: a sagebrush field experiment showed deep water raised surface 15N cycling and respiration, and grass pots with lift blocked showed lower decomposition, so the mechanism has direct analogues. Risk: trenching and root exclusion confound lift with root death and loss of root exudates, and in trees lift volumes may be too small to matter or moisture may favour microbial N immobilisation over mineralisation, which could cancel or flip the net mineralisation signal.
title: Night root water lift speeds soil nitrogen release

untested: A clean forested-versus-sparse basin contrast of runoff ratio against CO2 with precipitation, temperature, land use and leaf area as covariates, backed by FACE sap-flow checks, is not settled; the global catchment attribution found near-zero median CO2 effect, so the predicted runoff-ratio rise is not detected.

papers.title: Global climate model with a vegetation component: physiological forcing from doubled CO2 raised simulated global runoff by about 6%; a model projection, not an observed basin trend

Catchment-scale attribution across 1116 unimpacted catchments, 1981-2020, constrained by observed streamflow: median direct CO2 contribution approached zero; the opposite of a detectable decades-long runoff-ratio rise

web.text: Models predict higher runoff from CO2-driven stomatal closure, but observation-constrained catchment analyses find the net effect is close to zero because greater leaf area and growth offset the lower conductance. Other work argues the effect depends on aridity, so the sign can differ by climate.

links.label: Direct CO2 effect on streamflow, Nat Commun 2024

why: Strength: stomatal closure under high CO2 is measured at FACE sites and models give about 6% more runoff at doubled CO2. Risk: a 1116-catchment attribution found a near-zero median direct CO2 effect, and greening-driven leaf area growth offsets lower conductance, and because CO2, temperature and leaf area all trend together the regression cannot cleanly isolate CO2 so the sign is a net of opposed mechanisms.
title: Rising CO2 raises river runoff ratio

untested: The size and persistence of the effect for atmospheric deposition specifically (as opposed to fertilizer additions) at chronic low doses, and in which soils the response saturates or declines, are less clear; the core N-raises-phosphatase link is already established.

papers.title: Meta-analysis of 34 studies: N fertilization enhanced phosphatase activity from tropics to extra-tropics, in roots and bulk soil, while P fertilization suppressed it; mostly fertilizer, not deposition gradients
Letter on long-term N addition: N stimulation of soil phosphatase appears to decline progressively with years of N addition, citing a long-term chaparral-type record; indicates the effect can fade
7-year simulated N deposition in calcareous grassland raised root-surface phosphomonoesterase activity in three plant functional types; plant roots not bulk soil

web.text: A multi-biome meta-analysis finds N addition raises phosphatase activity, and deposition-simulation experiments show the same in plant roots. Evidence that the stimulation can fade with decades of N addition means the direction holds but the long-term size is uncertain.

links.label: Deposition and root phosphatase, calcareous grassland

why: Strength: a 34-study meta-analysis found N addition raised phosphatase activity from tropics to extra-tropics, and a 7-year simulated deposition experiment raised root phosphatase. Risk: the link is already established so there is almost nothing new, and long-term N addition can fade or erase the stimulation, so only the size and persistence, not the direction, are in doubt.
title: Nitrogen deposition raises soil phosphatase activity

untested: Validation against deep hydrographic sections and abyssal temperature trends with modern flux maps and eddy-resolving or multi-model comparisons is incomplete; existing numbers come from one global model configuration and the Arctic deep-warming signal exceeds what geothermal heating explains.

papers.title: Ocean model with no, uniform and spatially varying geothermal heat flux: with strong mixing the AABW cell strengthened about 15% (2.5 Sv), deep North Pacific warmed up to 0.3 C and Southern Ocean poleward heat transport rose about 10%; single model, climatological data

Deep Arctic Ocean warming observed at 0.020 C/decade exceeds what geothermal heating explains; attributes the excess to heat transferred from the deep Atlantic; does not test global overturning with and without geothermal flux
Coupled climate model preprint: geothermal heating weakens deep stratification and strengthens AABW and deepens the AMOC in the Last Glacial Maximum, with a different sea-ice response today; preprint

web.text: Emile-Geay and Madec ran ocean model pairs with and without spatially varying geothermal heat flux and reported about a 15% stronger AABW cell and about 10% more Southern Ocean poleward heat transport, almost exactly the stated estimate. What remains is observational validation and robustness across models.

why: Strength: Emile-Geay and Madec 2009 ran exactly these with and without spatially varying geothermal flux and found about 15% stronger AABW cell and 10% more Southern Ocean heat transport, matching the stated 10-15%. Risk: the result depends on the mixing parameterization and a single model, but the sign of added bottom heat weakening stratification is robust; little remains beyond observational validation.
title: Geothermal heat flux strengthens deep ocean overturning in models

untested: No study found pairing debris-rich and debris-poor glacier catchments and linking dust grain size and mineralogy to the weathering or erosion rate of surrounding rock; existing work shows dust and local moraine sources matter at single glaciers but does not test the weathering-rate dependence or the 1-9 W/m2 range.

papers.title: Vadret da Morteratsch: summer albedo fell 0.32 to 0.15 after 2003 from mineral and biogenic dust, ~3.5 m extra ice loss over 2003-06 (equal to +1.7 K air temperature); moraine dust named as an important feedback; one glacier, no weathering-rate link
Argentiere Glacier model: Saharan dust cut annual mass balance by 0.31-0.45 m w.e. and accounted for about 8-16% of summer melt; long-range dust, modelled, no catchment debris or weathering analysis

web.text: Dust on glaciers, including dust from exposed moraines and bedrock, lowers albedo and speeds melt, with effects ranging from small to large by site and a tropical Andes study finding under 1% reflectivity loss. The specific dependence on weathering intensity of the surrounding catchment is not tested.

why: Strength: dust darkening of glaciers is documented (Morteratsch albedo fell 0.32 to 0.15, with moraine dust named as a source). Risk: dust supply depends on wind, source exposure and snow cover more than weathering rate, and thick supraglacial debris insulates ice and slows melt, which could reverse the sign for the most debris-rich glaciers.
title: Rockier glacier catchments give darker ice and faster melt

untested: No study found regressing dust immersion-freezing temperature against a weathering index (such as CIA) with measured feldspar content; existing work characterises pure feldspars and shows feldspar dominates dust ice nucleation, not how source-soil weathering changes it. Biological and organic ice nucleators in soil dust can mask feldspar at warmer temperatures.

papers.title: Droplet-freezing assays: feldspar, especially K-feldspar, dominates ice nucleation by mineral dust at mixed-phase conditions despite being a minor component, clays unimportant; did not vary source weathering intensity

Survey of 15 feldspars: K-rich alkali feldspars usually nucleate ice better than Ca-bearing plagioclase, large within-group variability, some activity loss when aged in water (about 2 C for hyper-active K-feldspar over 16 months); pure minerals, not weathered soil dusts
Perthite feldspar powders: onset -2 to -4 C and site populations tied to exsolution and microcline structure; industrial powders, no weathering gradient

web.text: Feldspar content and structure control mineral-dust ice nucleation, and ageing in water lowers activity somewhat, so weathering that removes K-feldspar should reduce activity. I found no measurement along a weathering-intensity gradient, and the size of a few degrees C shift is untested.

why: Strength: K-feldspar dominates mineral-dust ice nucleation and feldspar loses about 2 C of activity when aged in water, so removing it by weathering should warm-limit freezing. Risk: soil dust also carries biological and organic ice nucleators that act at warmer temperatures, and weathering can leave K-feldspar as a resistant residue, either of which could flip or flatten the trend with the weathering index.
title: Weathered source dust freezes at colder temperatures

untested: Direct 14C-dead CO2 measurements in soil gas and river water along an erosion-rate gradient on shale, with microbial-inhibitor incubations, are only partly done; the heat released by rock organic carbon respiration is not measured or shown to matter.

papers.title: Taiwan Central Range soils: on average 67% of bedrock OCpetro oxidised in soils, CO2 emission 6.1-18.6 t C/km2/yr rising with erosion rate; microbial mediation shown by lipid biomarkers and isotopes; did not use inhibitors or measure heat

Rhenium-based global catchment extrapolation: rock organic carbon oxidation releases CO2 rivalling or exceeding silicate weathering drawdown, hotspots in uplifted fine-grained sedimentary mountains; flux estimate from rhenium, not direct respiration

web.text: Rhenium and biomarker work shows rock organic carbon is oxidised in soils and rivers with fluxes that rise with erosion rate, and that oxidation is microbially mediated. The global flux estimate and Taiwan share match the stated figures in kind, while respiration heat and inhibitor-controlled incubations are not reported.

why: Strength: Hemingway 2018 found 67% of bedrock rock organic carbon oxidised in Taiwan soils with CO2 rising with erosion rate (6.1-18.6 t C/km2/yr), and Zondervan 2023 extrapolated globally, so the direction is measured. Risk: the claim is largely published, the heat-release part is trivial and unmeasurable, and abiotic oxidation could account for part of the CO2 so inhibitor incubations may show less microbial share, though erosion-dependence would still hold.
title: Eroding black shale releases rock carbon as CO2

untested: A matched-hillslope comparison with different weathering depth and fracture density at equal rainfall, scaling dry-season transpiration share (the 10-30% of annual rainfall estimate) with fracture density and weathering depth, is not found; existing work shows bedrock water use is widespread but not how it scales across sites.

papers.title: Continental-US estimate of bedrock-water contribution to transpiration: woody plants routinely access rock moisture, not only in drought; lower-bound estimate from datasets, no matched-hillslope or fracture-density scaling
Direct observation of rock moisture in a weathered-bedrock hillslope: weathered zone tens of metres thick stores water that plants draw down; one site, no cross-site comparison with unfractured rock
Review of bedrock as a tree water reservoir under drought: notes uncertainty on pathways and efficiency of rock-root exchange; synthesis not a matched test

web.text: Several studies show trees draw on water stored in weathered or fractured bedrock, especially in dry seasons, and that this is widespread. The dose-response with fracture density and the specific transpiration share are not established.

why: Strength: trees routinely draw on rock moisture (McCormick 2021) and weathered zones tens of metres thick store water that plants draw down (Rempe and Dietrich 2018). Risk: matching hillslopes for rainfall, species and rooting depth is difficult and the 10-30% of rainfall figure is a guess, and thick weathered rock can instead feed deep drainage or lower runoff, which would leave the transpired share unchanged.
title: Fractured weathered bedrock raises dry-season tree transpiration

untested: Whether films of surfactant (surface-active molecules) that build up during lake algal blooms cut the gas transfer velocity for CO2 and methane by 20-50% at the same wind speed, so that wind-based models overestimate bloom-period gas release by roughly 1.3-2 times. The effect is established at sea; the lake version is untested.

papers.title: Mustaffa et al. 2020: gas transfer 23% lower above 200 ug Teq/L surfactant and 62% lower in slicks, including a Trichodesmium bloom (all marine)
Pereira et al. 2016: lab tank with coastal water showed 14-51% suppression of gas transfer (marine; no blooms or freshwater)
Khan et al. 2026, Lake Stechlin: calls surfactant suppression plausible but untested (no surfactant measurements)
Karnatz et al. 2026: surfactants rise under cyanobacteria-dominated conditions at sea (no gas transfer measured)

web.text: Surfactant films are well shown to slow gas exchange at sea, and blooms raise surfactants. No study measured it in lakes: only 8 papers combine microlayer, gas transfer and film terms, and none are on topic. A 2021 cruise analysis reportedly found no chlorophyll-surfactant link, and bloom pH and CO2 drawdown change flux separately from the transfer velocity.

why: Strength: surfactants cut gas transfer 14-62% in marine tank and field work, and blooms raise surfactants, with a clear k600 slope falsification at about 10%. Risk: lake bloom surfactant has never been measured against gas transfer, and bloom wind-sheltering, changed turbulence and bloom pH drawdown could mask the film effect or even raise apparent k600, and one cruise analysis found no chlorophyll-surfactant link.
title: Algal bloom films slow gas exchange in lakes

untested: Whether, over rock rich in oxidizing iron-bearing minerals (biotite granite, quartz diorite, gneiss), the depth to which trees draw seasonal rock moisture follows the depth of the biotite-oxidation and fracture front, and is shallower over biotite-poor rock. No study measured both together.

papers.title: Holbrook et al. 2019: a 65 m borehole shows iron loss and fractured, expanded biotite from about 38 m, with fracture density rising from about 4% to 16% (no roots or moisture measured)
Napieralski et al. 2019: iron-oxidizing bacteria oxidize biotite iron in lab incubations of crushed rock (no fracturing, flow or roots)
Rempe and Dietrich 2018: rock moisture is about 4.7 times soil moisture, with roots seen to 16 m (rock types not compared)
Crutchfield-Peters et al. 2025: trees draw bedrock water to about 7 m (no mineral oxidation measured)

web.text: Each side is documented: biotite oxidation fractures rock, and trees use water stored in weathered rock. A search for biotite together with rock moisture found nothing. Counter-evidence: rock moisture also sits in older tectonic fractures and clay-rich rock, and iron loss may be a result of water flowing along fractures, not their cause.

why: Strength: biotite oxidation is shown to fracture rock (Holbrook 2019, fracture density 4% to 16%) and trees do draw rock moisture to about 7-16 m, so each link is real. Risk: the chain needs oxidation to set porosity and roots to follow it, while iron loss may be a result of flow along tectonic fractures and clay-rich rock stores water too, and the test must separate oxidation from fracture density with only a few 15-30 m wells, so the sign could flip if drawdown tracks fracture density alone.
title: How deep iron minerals have oxidized sets how deep trees draw rock water
Forest spore ice nuclei glaciate clouds warmer than ocean air
untested: No study links wet-night spore INP enhancement over forest to warmer cloud-top glaciation temperature or a larger ice-rain share versus dust-free ocean air; the 10x and 2-5 C magnitudes are untested and confounded by aerosol, dynamics and cloud-top height.

papers.title: Bioaerosols (fluorescent biological particles) were the main INP source at -12 to -20 C in coastal California; tested INP speciation and model skill, not cloud-phase response or rain ice fraction
Convective-storm study in Colorado: rain raised fungal spore counts and measured INPs alongside; did not link to cloud-top phase or compare forest vs ocean
Satellite T* (mixed-phase transition temperature) shifts with snow/sea-ice cover, showing surface INP sources influence cloud phase at high latitudes; did not look at forest or biological INPs
Eastern Mediterranean orographic clouds: INPs show diurnal cycle driven by fluorescent bioaerosol; no forest-versus-ocean glaciation contrast

web.text: Biological INPs dominate the -12 to -20 C range in several continental and coastal settings, rain and humid nights raise fungal spore and INP loads, and satellite work shows surface INP sources can shift cloud-phase transition temperature. The specific chain from spore INPs to warmer cloud-top glaciation over forest and a higher ice-rain share has not been measured, and cloud-top phase is strongly affected by updraft strength and other aerosol.

why: Strength: bioaerosols were the main INP source at -12 to -20 C in coastal California and rain raises spore INP loads. Risk: the chain has several uncertain links (10x INP rise, 2-5 C warmer glaciation, larger ice-rain share) and cloud-top phase depends on updraft strength and cloud-top height, and in clouds where INPs are already abundant or secondary ice production dominates, extra spore INPs may not shift glaciation temperature.

title: Deforestation raises river silica and favours coastal diatoms
untested: The catchment half (more dissolved silica after clearing) has been measured at Hubbard Brook; what is untested is whether the extra silica raises Si:N at river mouths and shifts coastal phytoplankton toward diatoms, and whether this holds for cropland conversion, where fertiliser N and dams may reverse it.

papers.title: Hubbard Brook clear-cut raised stream dissolved silicate loss (Conley et al.); did not follow silica downstream to coastal phytoplankton (abstract not opened in full, record page redirected to Wiley)

untested: Models and chamber work already give this mechanism, but a matched observational comparison of measured CCN at 0.2 percent supersaturation in monsoon outflow versus low-NH3 convective outflow, binned by NH3 and SO2, is missing, as is a cloud radiative effect attributed to NH3 beyond sulfate.

title: Falling acid-rain sulfate changed lake phosphorus release by sediment Fe:S
untested: No paired-core or dated-core study of softwater lakes has tested whether post-1990 sulfate decline raised anoxic P release where porewater Fe:S is above 1 and lowered it where below 1; the 20 percent threshold and Fe:S breakpoint of 1 are untested.

title: Falling SO2 lowers aerosol iron solubility over iron-limited oceans
