Process model of enhanced rock weathering with ecohydrology and soil moisture; no surface-albedo term.

web.text: Biochar work shows that dark amendments at 30 t/ha cut soil albedo enough to erode a measurable share of climate benefit. Enhanced weathering trials and models report cation loss, yield and CDR but no albedo effect. Searches of Europe PMC for enhanced weathering together with soil or surface albedo give only a handful of unrelated hits.

why: Strength: Biochar at 30 t/ha cut albedo from 0.21 to 0.06, and dark basalt fines on a light soil at 25-50 t/ha must lower bare-soil albedo for as long as they sit on the surface, a simple optical effect. Risk: fresh-ground basalt can be pale grey and the darkening on a dark Mollisol may be under 0.02, and rain crusting or wet-soil darkening of the control could shrink the contrast, though the sign on light soil should hold.

title: Basalt dust on snow melts fields out earlier
untested: No trial has put crushed basalt on snowpack at agricultural rates, or measured melt-out timing, frozen-soil runoff losses and basalt recovery in runoff. Whether enhanced weathering operators spread on snow at all is unverified.

papers.title: Colorado River runoff under dust radiative forcing in snow: peak runoff about 3 weeks earlier with heavier dust; modelled, not a basalt or farm trial.
Four-year basalt field trial in the US Corn Belt (fall application); no snow, albedo or melt measurements.

web.text: Dust on snow lowers albedo and advances melt by weeks in mountain snowpacks, so the physics is established at much lower loads. No enhanced weathering paper addresses spreading on snow-covered or frozen ground; the combined Europe PMC query returns few hits and none on this.

why: Strength: dust on snow already advances melt by 18-35 days at far lower loads (Painter 2010, about 3 weeks earlier peak runoff), and 1-5 kg/m2 of basalt of albedo 0.1-0.2 is a thin dark layer, so melt-out should come earlier and the plot trial has a clear 3-day falsification threshold. Risk: the practice of spreading on snow is unverified, and a thick or buried layer could insulate snow and delay melt, which would reverse the sign, while under 1% runoff recovery is a second way to fail.

title: Air pollution haze slows UV breakdown of dryland litter
untested: Nobody has tested whether aerosol attenuation of UV and sunlight changes litter photodegradation, with filters mimicking haze spectra or along natural haze gradients. Haze also adds diffuse light and dust that could offset the UV loss.

papers.title: UNEP assessment chapter on UV, climate and terrestrial ecosystems, covering UV-driven litter breakdown; treats aerosol only generally and tests no haze-litter link.
12-month litterbag test of UV-B on wheat and maize straw (UV-B raised mass loss 14-19% without soil contact); did not vary aerosols or haze.

web.text: Many exclusion experiments show sunlight and UV raise litter mass loss, so a smaller dose should slow it. Reviews of UV effects note that clouds and ozone modulate exposure but I found no study linking aerosol load to litter photodegradation.

why: Strength: UV-B blocking cut Patagonian litter decomposition by 33% and full sunlight blocking by 60%, so a 20-40% UV cut from haze should slow photodegradation, and filter litterbags are standard. Risk: haze effects are smaller than cloud and season variation and microbial decay dominates many sites, and since haze adds diffuse light and dust that may speed biotic decay, total mass loss could be unchanged even if photochemical CO2 falls.

title: Cracks in dry Vertisols boost atmospheric methane uptake
untested: No study has measured CH4 flux over open versus closed shrinkage cracks in a Vertisol, or crack-wall methanotroph activity. The claim of a 2-5x uptake boost is untested.

papers.title: Conference abstract: nighttime thermal convection in soil fractures enhances gas flux, suggested for CO2 in clayey soils; did not measure methane.
Review of soil-aquifer processes under Vertisols: cracks as preferential flow and evaporation paths; methane not addressed.

web.text: Cracks are known to speed gas transport and to ventilate soil by thermal convection, but only CO2 and oxygen studies exist. I found no methane uptake measurement tied to crack state in Vertisols; the topic overlap in Europe PMC is about 2 papers.

why: Strength: cracks are known to ventilate soil by thermal convection and expose oxic wall surface, and open cracks versus wetted closed cracks on the same soil give a direct paired comparison with a 30% falsification threshold. Risk: no methane measurement exists and desiccation may water-stress methanotrophs in the dry matrix, or crack air may carry methane out from deeper layers, so a 2-5 fold boost may shrink to no difference.

title: Volcanic acid fallout starves nitrogen fixers of molybdenum
untested: Mo availability and free-living nitrogen fixation have not been measured along a volcanic acid-deposition transect. The Masaya work covers pH, bases, sulfate, chloride and fluoride but not Mo.

papers.title: Mo and P co-limit free-living N fixation in Panamanian forests; shows Mo availability controls fixation but involves no volcanic acid or pH gradient.
Masaya Andosols exposed to volcanic acid: pH and base cations fall, sulfate and fluoride retained, HCl main acidifier; no Mo or N fixation data.

web.text: Mo limits free-living fixation and molybdate sorption rises as pH falls, both well known. But the Masaya soils are mainly acidified by HCl, and retained sulfate competes with molybdate for sorption sites, which could raise rather than lower available Mo. No test of the link was found.

why: Strength: Mo limits free-living fixation (Panama co-limitation) and molybdate sorption rises as pH falls, and the Masaya transect with a Mo-addition factorial is a sharp test. Risk: Masaya soils are mainly acidified by HCl and retained sulfate competes with molybdate for sorption sites, which could raise available Mo, and volcanic Mo input could do the same, so the 30-70% Mo drop could reverse sign; the chain also has three uncertain links.

title: Clay-fixed ammonium weakens fertiliser inhibition of methane uptake
untested: No study has compared ammonium inhibition of atmospheric-level methane oxidation across vermiculitic, illitic and kaolinitic soils, or tested K-blocked versus Ca-vermiculite. Ammonium fixation has not been linked to methanotroph inhibition.

papers.title: Ammonium and non-ammonium salts cut forest-soil methane uptake largely through ion exchange displacing ammonium; clay mineralogy and ammonium fixation not tested.
Review of nitrogen as a regulator of methane oxidation (inhibition, but also N limitation); no treatment of clay-fixed ammonium.

web.text: Ammonium inhibition of upland methane uptake is well documented and exchange-site behaviour already shapes it. Ammonium fixation by 2:1 clays is a separate, well-known soil process. The two literatures barely meet: a combined Europe PMC search finds only a few papers, none testing clay type.

why: Strength: 2:1 clays fix NH4+ within hours, and the sand plus vermiculite or kaolinite design with K-saturated controls cleanly isolates clay type with a stated falsification rule. Risk: exchange displacement is already known to drive inhibition, and fixed NH4+ can be re-released and nitrite from methanotroph ammonia oxidation may cause inhibition independent of soil-solution NH4+, which could make inhibition equal across clays.

title: Large soil aggregates have anoxic cores that release iron-bound phosphate
untested: Nobody has mapped Fe(II) and labile P against aggregate size and anoxic volume in one aerobic upland soil, with crushing as a control. Aggregate-size P studies exist but do not link release to anoxic cores.

papers.title: Phosphorus fractions across aggregate sizes under rice, maize and soybean: Fe/Al-bound P concentrated in large aggregates and shifted under aerobic-anaerobic cycling; no oxygen mapping or Fe(II) test.
Review of anoxic microsites and their role in Fe, N and C cycles; conceptual, no aggregate-size P experiment.

web.text: Anoxic microsites and Fe-driven P mobilisation under reducing conditions are both established, and large aggregates retain Fe-bound P. The specific claim that aggregate interiors under moist but drained conditions release P in proportion to anoxic volume is not directly shown. Overlap in Europe PMC is about 2 papers.

why: Strength: Anoxic microsites and Fe(III) reduction releasing sorbed P are both established, and the crushed-aggregate control plus optode and DGT imaging isolates the mechanism. Risk: at 65% water-filled pore space most 8-16 mm aggregates may stay oxic so Fe(II) does not rise, and released P can re-sorb to Fe oxides or be masked by organic P, which would flip or erase the 2-5x contrast.

title: Nitrate-fed roots precipitate calcite in the rhizosphere of calcareous soils
untested: Nobody has compared rhizosphere carbonate content and delta-13C between nitrate- and ammonium-fed roots in calcareous soil. Root respiration CO2 may push the opposite way and dissolve calcite.

papers.title: Nitrate raised rhizosphere pH by 0.19-0.78 units and ammonium lowered it by 0.16-0.38 in wheat and lupin; priming effect studied, carbonate not.
Incubations show organic residue decomposition acidifies soil and dissolves calcite via respired CO2; no plants or N form comparison.

web.text: Nitrate alkalinisation and ammonium acidification at roots are well documented. Whether this crosses calcite saturation, given high rhizosphere CO2 and bicarbonate buffering, is unshown; recent work stresses respiration-driven carbonate dissolution. I found no rhizolith or rhizosheath study tied to N form.

why: Strength: nitrate raised rhizosphere pH by 0.19-0.78 and ammonium lowered it by 0.16-0.38 in wheat and lupin, so a nitrate-versus-ammonium carbonate contrast has a direct pH basis, and rhizobox calcimetry with d13C is standard. Risk: respired root CO2 and bicarbonate buffering could keep the solution below calcite saturation (the 2025 incubations show biogenic CO2 dissolves calcite), and then nitrate-fed rhizosphere would show no net precipitation, and the test fails if carbonate differs by under 5%.

title: Snow reflects UV onto standing litter and speeds its breakdown
untested: No experiment has used real snow with UV-transparent versus UV-blocking films on standing litter. The only albedo test used artificial surfaces and found a small effect.

papers.title: Sorghum litter over aluminium, white and black surfaces mimicking snow: 1.4-2.5% more mass loss over the UV-reflective surface; snow itself never tested.
Five-month desert litter study with warming and added winter snow cover; looked at decomposition rate, not UV reflection.
UNEP assessment chapter covering UV-driven litter breakdown; snow reflection only speculative.

web.text: Photodegradation of standing litter is well documented and snow reflectance has been proposed as an amplifier. The one albedo test showed only a few percent extra mass loss, much smaller than the 8-20% predicted. No snow trial exists.

why: Strength: the black-cloth control and UV-transparent versus Mylar films isolate snow reflection directly, and fresh snow reflects 0.8-0.9 of UV. Risk: the only albedo test gave 1.4-2.5% extra mass loss, far under the predicted 8-20%, so the 5% falsifier may fail even if the direction holds, and cold dry litter plus low winter UV or snowmelt wetting that boosts microbial decay could mask or reverse the effect.

title: Snowmelt-dominated soils carry carbonate deeper than rain-fed soils
untested: No pedon-database regression has isolated snow fraction on depth to the carbonate horizon at fixed precipitation and temperature. Cold-water calcite solubility versus infiltration depth has not been separated in columns.

papers.title: Seasonal bias in pedogenic carbonate formation in central New Mexico soils (I could read only the title and record); concerns timing, not snow versus rain depth.
Process model of soil inorganic carbon under climate change with daily water balance; no snow fraction test of carbonate depth.

web.text: Carbonate depth is known to relate to precipitation and seasonality, but depth-rainfall relations are weak and contested in the literature. Snowmelt infiltrating at low evapotranspiration should wet deeper. I found no direct test of the snow fraction effect; overlap in Europe PMC is about 4 papers.

links.label: Breecker et al. seasonal carbonate record

why: Strength: snowmelt infiltrating at near-zero evapotranspiration wets 2-3 times deeper than the same water as summer rain, and the NRCS pedon database with PRISM covariates and a +3 cm per 10% snow threshold makes a clean regression. Risk: carbonate depth also records dust input, parent material and paleoclimate inheritance that can swamp a 10-30 cm effect, and cold-climate leaching that removes carbonate could reverse the apparent sign in snowy sites.

title: Clear nights deposit more dew on litter and speed night decay
untested: No study has binned nights by longwave loss or used a longwave-opaque shelter to show cloud cover gates litter wetness and night-time CO2 efflux. Dew studies on litter exist but without this cloud link.

papers.title: Namib litter: fungi respond within minutes to fog and dew moisture and decompose surface litter; cloud or longwave control not examined.
Standing grass litter fungi and decomposition under non-rainfall versus rain moisture regimes in the Namib; no radiative driver.
Global eddy covariance evidence for soil water vapour adsorption at high humidity; not litter, no cloud test.

web.text: Non-rainfall moisture is known to activate litter decay in drylands, and radiative cooling under clear skies is the textbook dew mechanism. The link between nocturnal cloud, litter moisture and respiration has not been measured; counts show only about 2 overlapping papers.

why: Strength: radiative cooling under clear skies driving dew is textbook physics, litter fungi respond within minutes to dew (Namib work), and the binned-night design with a longwave-opaque shelter is directly diagnostic. Risk: hygroscopic water uptake can wet litter without dew at RH below 80%, so the 2-3 times difference could shrink, and overcast nights often bring higher RH which could offset the cloud effect.

title: Atmospheric rivers raise winter ocean CO2 uptake despite warming
untested: Nobody has composited air-sea CO2 flux at Station Papa on atmospheric-river days or measured the net of faster gas exchange against surface warming. Only storm studies from tropical cyclones and AR-marine heatwave studies exist.

papers.title: Tropical cyclone wind-pump effect on pCO2 and air-sea CO2 flux at two moorings; tropical storms, not atmospheric rivers or Papa.
Atmospheric rivers cool through cloud and warm through reduced heat loss, shaping marine heatwaves; no carbon flux analysed.
Storm-resolving model: tropical cyclones boost CO2 flux 20-40 times and cool the surface; not atmospheric rivers.

web.text: Storm studies show wind-driven gas exchange dominates, and AR work confirms opposing cloud and heat-flux effects on SST. No paper combines them for CO2; strict searches for atmospheric rivers with air-sea CO2 flux return near zero relevant hits.

why: Strength: wind speed of 12-18 m/s versus 8-9 m/s gives a 2-3 fold rise in k (scaling with wind squared) against only a 10-25 percent cut in the air-sea gradient from 0.2-0.5 C warming, using the Papa mooring record since 2010. Risk: AR days are few in number and rain freshening, mixed-layer deepening, and storm entrainment of CO2-rich subsurface water could raise surface pCO2 enough to cancel uptake, and an AR share of 25-40 percent is a magnitude that may not hold.

title: Dam-cut river sediment slows carbon sinking on river-fed margins
untested: No experiment or trap comparison has tied river sediment decline after damming to lithogenic ballast and carbon transfer on the adjacent slope. Most river sediment settles on the shelf, so the signal at 500-1000 m may be tiny.

papers.title: Mineral ballast in surface export from thorium data: ballast matters most in the North Atlantic, unballasted export often dominates; no rivers or dams.
Clay added to seawater raised TEP tenfold and formed sinking organoclay flocs; microcosm, no river loads or respiration per metre.
Review of large-river delta fronts, Changjiang and Mississippi, as recorders of human change; discusses carbon fluxes, not ballast or dams.

web.text: Ballast effects on sinking are well known but vary strongly by region, and sediment-load decline after damming is well documented. The two have not been joined in an experiment or trap comparison.

why: Strength: Lithogenic ballast raised lab aggregate sinking speed by about 150%, and sediment load falls after dams are well documented, so the roller-tank loading contrast is clear. Risk: most river sediment settles on the shelf so the 500-1000 m signal may be tiny, and lithogenic particles also promote flocculation and organoclay formation, so lower loads could leave transfer efficiency unchanged or even increase it.

title: Ocean acidification cuts sea-to-air methylamine emissions
untested: Nobody has measured how seawater pH changes amine emission to air, or the dissolved-to-gas ratio across pH 7.7-8.1. Biological changes in amine supply could offset the chemistry.

papers.title: Review of ocean acidification effects on DMS, N2O, ammonia and halocarbons; amines not quantified.
Flux-system study of ammonia and amines from model aqueous solutions with CIMS; shows Henry's-law uncertainty, no pH series or seawater.

web.text: Amine protonation at seawater pH follows acid-base equilibrium, and the volatile fraction does fall as pH drops. Reviews cover OA effects on ammonia and DMS, but I found no pH-controlled seawater amine flux measurement. Henry's-law constants for amines are uncertain by orders of magnitude.

links.label: OA and marine trace gases review

why: Strength: at fixed total amine the unprotonated fraction follows Henderson-Hasselbalch with pKa 9.8-10.7, so pH 8.1 to 7.9 cuts volatile fraction by about 35-37%, a well-measured acid-base relation with a lab test that has a 15% falsification band. Risk: Henry's-law constants for amines are uncertain by orders of magnitude and the real-ocean amine supply could rise or fall with plankton change, and warming adds about 7% per C, so net ocean emission could move the other way even if the fixed-total chemistry holds.

title: Fine volcanic ash suppresses soil methane uptake
untested: No study has measured methane uptake under graded ash thickness and grain size on upland soil. Sulfate and fluoride toxicity versus diffusion blockage is unseparated.

papers.title: PhD thesis on volcanic sulfate and fluoride on soil gas fluxes: tephra-like sulfate and fluoride doses did not change peat CH4 flux; a wet ash layer slowed CO2 release; not upland methane uptake.
Review of methane cycling in temperate forests; soils are sinks with varying controls, no volcanic ash effect.

web.text: Upland methane uptake is controlled by gas diffusion, and wet fine layers and compaction cut it. Ash effects have been studied for CO2 and peat chemistry but not for atmospheric methane uptake.

links.label: Myers thesis, volcanic S and F on soil gas

why: Strength: high-affinity methanotroph uptake is diffusion-limited and compaction cuts it about 90%, so a wet fine ash layer with air-filled porosity under 0.1 should throttle it, and capped cores need no eruption. Risk: the 60-95% cut and the net methane source claim are strong, and ash that dries and cracks or soluble sulfate and fluoride could change the response, so field results after a rare ashfall may differ from the lab caps.

title: Fresh labile carbon primes rock organic carbon oxidation
untested: No incubation has partitioned CO2 from shale with and without labile carbon by 14C and 13C, nor tested priming of kerogen in sterile controls. Rock carbon oxidation studies have not added labile carbon.

papers.title: Model of shale regolith carbon: petrogenic and pyrite oxidation CO2 smaller than soil respiration fluxes; no priming experiment.
Rhenium tracing shows glaciated catchments oxidise rock-bound organic carbon 2-3 times faster; no labile carbon test.
Goldschmidt 2023 abstract on two-stage oxidation of petrogenic carbon (priming suggested; I could only read the title).

web.text: Petrogenic carbon oxidation is microbially mediated and priming is common for young soil carbon. Work on kerogen mostly addresses temperature, erosion and water. I found no experiment adding labile carbon to shale.

why: Strength: 13C-glucose plus 14C-dead CO2 partitioning with gamma-irradiated controls cleanly separates petrogenic CO2 from added and native carbon, and no joint literature exists (0 hits). Risk: aromatic kerogen is highly recalcitrant and microbes fed glucose may use it instead of rock carbon, giving no or negative priming, and the 20% threshold at 120 days could be missed because petrogenic CO2 is a small share of total flux.

title: Sulfate from glacial pyrite oxidation suppresses lake methane emission
untested: No survey of proglacial lakes has compared methane emission by bedrock sulfide content, or run molybdate slurry tests. Lithology is confounded with organic carbon, depth and glacier cover.

papers.title: Synthesis of proglacial lake methane fluxes in Alaska and Greenland; sulfate and lithology not examined.
Tibetan proglacial lake sediments: methane oxidation and sulfide-oxidising methanotroph genomes; no emission or lithology comparison.
Peat mesocosm dosed with volcanic sulfate: no significant change in CH4 flux, against earlier reports of suppression.

web.text: Sulfate reducers outcompeting methanogens is textbook, and glacial sulfide oxidation makes sulfate-rich water. Proglacial lake methane work exists, but none compares lithology or sulfate. A peat dosing test found no sulfate effect, so the suppression is not guaranteed.

why: Strength: sulfate reducers outcompeting methanogens above roughly 0.1 mmol/L sulfate is textbook, and glacial sulfide oxidation gives sulfate-rich inflow; the molybdate slurry test is decisive. Risk: lithology is confounded with organic carbon, depth and glacier cover, proglacial lakes emit little methane anyway, and a peat dosing experiment found no sulfate effect, so organic carbon limitation could make the lithology classes indistinguishable.

title: Forest canopy cuts thermal-stress cracking of surface rock
untested: No paired shaded versus exposed boulder study has counted acoustic-emission cracking events or tested canopy removal. Temperature damping is documented, but cracking is not.

papers.title: Instrumented single granite boulder in full sun: nearly 12,000 acoustic emissions in four months, mostly as the rock cooled in the afternoon; no shaded control.
Ivy cover on limestone walls cut freezing events 26% and lab stone decay; frost not solar stress, and ivy not canopy.

web.text: Acoustic emission tracks solar-driven rock cracking and vegetation is reported to damp rock temperature swings. Whether canopy cuts actual cracking is unproven, and moisture under cover could add other cracking.

why: Strength: shade cuts the daily rock temperature range from 20-45 K to 5-12 K and heating rate from about 10 to 2-3 K per hour, and acoustic emission tracks solar-driven cracking (12,000 events in four months on a sunlit boulder). Risk: 12-24 months of AE monitoring on 6-10 boulder pairs is demanding and event counts could be sparse, and shaded rock stays wetter so moisture-driven or frost cracking could add events and push the shaded fraction above the 30 percent threshold.

title: Glacier-ground apatite bedrock boosts free-living N fixation
untested: No study has compared diazotroph activity (acetylene reduction or nifH) across glacier forelands or glacier-fed streams on contrasting bedrock types (apatite-bearing vs P-poor), nor run P/Mo additions on rock-flour soils to see how much of the gap closes.

papers.title: Large-scale N and P addition in early proglacial soils: P availability drove biological N fixation, but lithology of the bedrock was not varied
Glacial rock flour supplies bioavailable P, Fe and Mn to an Arctic alga within days; phytoplankton growth tested, not N fixation or bedrock contrasts
Glacial flour as soil amendment (Himalayan gneiss vs Icelandic basalt flour) with soybean; nutrient supply tested, not diazotrophs

web.text: Foreland chronosequence studies (Hailuogou, Damma, Arctic forefields) show nifH abundance rising with succession and correlating with available P, and a 2025 proglacial N and P addition experiment found P availability drives N fixation. Rock flour is known to release bioavailable P. None of these compare bedrock types, so the 2-5x lithology effect is untested.

why: Strength: P limits free-living N fixation in young proglacial soils (2025 N and P addition experiment) and rock flour releases bioavailable P, so apatite-rich bedrock plausibly raises fixation. Risk: bedrock P is confounded with pH, Fe, carbon and deglaciation age, and Mo or carbon can limit instead, while limestone also carries apatite, so the 2-5x lithology gap could be null or reversed.

title: N-rich bedrock lowers free-living nitrogen fixation
untested: The direction was tested and found opposite for free-living fixation in temperate forests; untested is the symbiotic/nodulation part, the fertilizer-equalization test, and whether the effect flips in other biomes.

papers.title: Dynarski et al.: forests on N-rich bedrock had HIGHER free-living N fixation than on N-poor rock, attributed to more soil C and P; did not test legume nodulation or tropical sites
Houlton et al.: bedrock N is a global N source (19-31 Tg N/yr mobilized); did not measure fixation response

web.text: The closest direct test (Dynarski et al. 2019) found free-living N fixation was higher on N-rich bedrock, because such sites accumulate more soil C and P that feed fixers. The proposed down-regulation by rock-derived mineral N is therefore opposed by published field data, though legumes could still respond differently.

why: Strength: the paired-catchment design with 15N2 or acetylene reduction and a fertilizer equalisation check is clear and can falsify the claim. Risk: Dynarski 2019 found free-living N fixation was higher on N-rich bedrock, because such soils hold more C and P that feed fixers, and that competing mechanism outweighs any nitrogenase down-regulation by rock-derived mineral N, so the predicted sign is opposed by field data.

title: N-rich rock lowers total forest nitrogen fixation
untested: Total (symbiotic plus free-living) fixation per area on rock-N gradients, 15N2 or nodule measurements, and regression on rock N weathered have not been reported; the one study found the opposite sign for free-living fixation.

papers.title: Dynarski et al.: free-living N fixation higher in forests on N-rich bedrock; symbiotic fixation and per-area totals not measured
Houlton et al.: global rock N weathering flux; no fixation response tested

web.text: Published field data show higher, not lower, free-living fixation on N-rich bedrock, explained by greater soil C and P. Whether symbiotic fixers respond the other way (as facultative fixers do under high soil N) remains open, but the headline 30-60% lower total fixation is not supported.

why: Strength: the design separates symbiotic and free-living fixation with 15N2 and d15N and regresses on rock N weathered. Risk: Dynarski 2019 found free-living fixation higher on N-rich bedrock, the opposite sign for half the pool, and the only route to a net decrease is a facultative symbiotic fixer drop under high soil N that would have to outweigh the free-living increase.

title: Volcanic ash ballasts marine snow and boosts deep carbon flux
untested: No study has measured sinking POC flux, lithogenic flux or marine-snow sinking speed at 500-1000 m before and after an ash fall, nor roller-tank tests of marine snow with added volcanic ash separating ballast from bloom effects.

papers.title: 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption: GEOTRACES South Pacific trace-metal and Nd-isotope input from ash; documented ash chemistry, not sinking flux or ballast
Ocean-colour analysis of phytoplankton carbon after Hunga Tonga; surface satellite anomalies only, no particle-flux data
Soviadan et al.: BGC-Argo imaging shows marine-snow morphology controls sinking speed and attenuation; ballast discussed but no ash or dust manipulation

web.text: Mineral ballast is well known to correlate with POC flux, and Saharan dust increases aggregate sinking in mesocosm work, so ash ballast is plausible. Eruption studies so far focus on iron and trace-metal fertilization and surface ocean colour, not sinking-particle flux, and ash can also be toxic or dissolve, which could cancel ballast.

why: Strength: mineral ballast is well known to correlate with POC flux and Saharan dust raised aggregate sinking in mesocosms, and roller-tank incubations with 1-10 mg per L ash are cheap. Risk: large eruptions over oligotrophic water are rare and unplanned, so the field trap test depends on luck, and ash toxicity, glass dissolution and bloom-driven changes could cancel ballast or confound a 1.5-3 times flux rise, which could flip or hide the sign.

title: Flood basalt eruptions raise marine phosphorus burial within 500 kyr
untested: No compilation compares P/Al or SEDEX phosphorus rise across multiple dated LIP onsets against non-LIP hyperthermals, with Hg timing and Os/Sr/Li weathering proxies, to test the 1.5-3x size and the lead-lag.

papers.title: Hg, conodont temperature and weathering proxies show volcanism and basalt weathering drove Ordovician cooling; one interval, not a multi-LIP P/Al comparison
Model of coupled marine P and atmospheric oscillation after end-Permian extinction; modelling, not P/Al across LIP onsets
Terrestrial forcing of marine biodiversification: links volcanism and nutrient runoff to marine diversification; coarse Phanerozoic scale

web.text: Hg-timed LIP records often show rising weathering and nutrient influx, and P-cycle models invoke enhanced P supply after Siberian Traps volcanism. But marine P burial after anoxia is also driven by P recycling from sediments, which can raise or lower P/Al independent of weathering, and Hg anomalies are patchy in shallow settings.

why: Strength: Hg anomalies, P/Al and Os/Sr/Li are measurable on existing sections with a lead-lag falsifier, and Hg-timed LIP records often show raised weathering and nutrient input. Risk: marine P burial after anoxia is controlled by sediment P recycling that can raise or lower P/Al independent of weathering, and the claim that LIP P rise exceeds non-LIP events of equal CO2 adds a second uncertain link, so redox-driven loss could reverse the sign.

title: High-alkalinity rivers slow coastal aragonite saturation decline
untested: No study regresses decadal change in coastal aragonite saturation on river alkalinity export across paired estuaries or shelves at matched freshwater fraction, or follows sites where river alkalinity changed (dams, liming, acid-rain recovery) to test the 30-60% buffering figure.

papers.title: Gulf of Maine boron-isotope pH record: pH rose with inflow of high-alkalinity Gulf Stream water, a buffering case but from ocean not river alkalinity
Mississippi Basin liming: century of river alkalinity flux records show lime raised alkalinity export with decadal lag; ocean carbonate chemistry not examined

web.text: It is well accepted that low-alkalinity freshwater makes coasts such as the Gulf of Maine poorly buffered and that organic alkalinity complicates estuary budgets. Direct quantitative tests of river alkalinity as a modifier of the decadal aragonite-saturation trend are lacking, and at matched freshwater fraction the effect is probably confined to plumes and low-salinity zones.

links.label: Delayed ocean acidification, Gulf of Maine

why: Strength: alkalinity buffers carbonate chemistry by established thermodynamics, and coastal acidification networks supply time series. Risk: at matched freshwater fraction the effect is probably confined to plumes, and high-alkalinity rivers also carry high DIC, pCO2 and nutrients, and organic alkalinity and eutrophication could make high-alkalinity coasts show equal or faster saturation loss.

title: Mineral CO2 adsorption drives dryland night-day soil CO2 flux
untested: A published study covers isotherms, Mojave field flux and hysteresis, but the abstract does not report sterilised-versus-live monolith chambers, a sand-versus-clay surface-area scaling test, or the specific 0.1-0.5 umol/m2/s magnitude and 10-30% Q10 change.

papers.title: Thermally driven CO2 adsorption/desorption and soil respiration: desert-soil isotherms plus Mojave field data show adsorption gives negative night and positive day flux and reverses apparent hysteresis; no sterilised monolith or soil-texture comparison reported
Abiotic reactions after wetting gamma-irradiated vs live dryland soil cores: abiotic N2O/NO emissions and partial CO2; tested wetting pulses, not diel temperature cycling of dry soil

web.text: A 2026 Science Advances paper reports that thermally driven CO2 adsorption/desorption on desert soil produces negative nocturnal and positive daytime flux, and that accounting for it reverses the apparent temperature hysteresis. The sterilisation and mineral-surface-area controls proposed here would be the confirmatory next steps rather than a new idea.

why: Strength: A 2026 Science Advances paper already shows desert-soil isotherms and Mojave flux with negative night and positive day CO2 flux from thermally driven adsorption, so the direction is directly measured. Risk: the core idea is published so only the sterilised monolith and sand-versus-clay scaling are new, and the 10-30% Q10 change depends on how much microbial flux the adsorption term is subtracted from.

title: Longer tundra zero-curtain means more cold-season carbon loss
untested: No study regresses Sept-May CO2 and CH4 flux on measured zero-curtain duration across tundra sites with snow depth, air temperature and moisture as covariates, or lengthens the plateau experimentally (snow fence or irrigation).

papers.title: GeoCryoAI maps circumarctic zero-curtain duration (100-4000 h) and says it sustains cold-season microbial activity; mapped timing, did not test flux response
Natali et al.: winter CO2 loss of 1662 Tg C/yr from permafrost region synthesized from in situ flux; tied to soil temperature, not zero-curtain duration
Long-term drainage and carbon fluxes from 8 years of eddy covariance at a permafrost site; hydrology effects, no zero-curtain metric

web.text: It is established that unfrozen water near 0 C keeps microbes active and that winter carbon loss is large and underestimated. The zero-curtain is proposed as the mechanism in review and mapping papers, but its duration has not been shown to predict cold-season CO2 plus CH4 better than snow depth or soil temperature.

why: Strength: existing eddy-covariance and soil-temperature records allow a direct regression, and unfrozen water near 0 C keeping microbes active is established, with winter loss of 1662 Tg C/yr. Risk: zero-curtain duration is confounded with snow insulation and soil water, so any link may reflect snow depth rather than latent heat, and the beyond-air-temperature claim needs a manipulation, and a longer plateau can also mean a colder deep freeze that lowers respiration, flipping the sign.

title: Night soil-vapour uptake switches on biocrust nitrogen fixation
untested: No study has run overnight acetylene reduction or 15N2 on crust cores with and without a vapour barrier on dew-free nights, or linked negative latent heat flux periods to nitrogenase activity.

papers.title: Eddy-covariance network shows soil water vapour adsorption (negative latent heat flux) occurs about 4 h per night, most in drylands; no biological activity measured
Negev lithic lichens: vapour distilled from wet soil after rain supplies much of their liquid water; tested hydration of lichens, not nitrogen fixation
Biocrust N fixation and exogenous P under N deposition; tested nutrient effects, not vapour-driven hydration

web.text: Soil vapour adsorption is now documented across dryland flux towers, and lichens use vapour-derived water. Biocrust nitrogenase studies I found all wet crusts with liquid water or rain, and vapour or dew alone was not tested as a trigger, so the claimed 2-5x activation is unsupported either way.

links.label: Soil water vapour adsorption, global flux towers
Distillation as water source, Negev lichens
Biocrust N fixation, P and N deposition

why: Strength: the vapour-barrier sealed film against open cores on dew-free nights is a clean design, and soil vapour adsorption now has a flux-tower record of about 4 h per night. Risk: biocrust nitrogenase has so far been triggered only by liquid water and needs light or carbon supply, so 1-2 cm of vapour wetting at 70-80% relative humidity may not hydrate cells, and the sealed film also changes temperature and gas exchange.

title: Soil nitrous acid shortens methane lifetime via extra OH
untested: Chemistry-climate runs with and without soil HONO already exist for ozone, but OH change and methane lifetime were not reported in the abstracts read, and no field dawn OH comparison over fertilized vs unfertilized plots was found.

papers.title: Global soil HONO emissions (9.4 to 11.5 Tg N, 1980-2016) in a chemistry-climate model raised surface O3 by 2.5%; abstract does not report OH or methane lifetime
Global soil HONO and PM2.5 over the last century with a process-based soil HONO module; air quality outcomes, not methane sink
Field fluxes and lab simulations: fertilizer-enhanced soil HONO emission at an agricultural site and the ozone-mitigation case; no OH measurement

web.text: Soil HONO as an OH precursor is established, and global models with soil HONO already exist, giving about 9-11 Tg N per year. Their reported effects are on ozone and PM2.5, so the specific methane-lifetime and global-OH change remains to be stated, and it is likely small relative to other OH sources.

why: Strength: HONO photolysis to OH is textbook, and adding a 9-11 Tg N per year OH source to a chemistry model must raise OH and shorten methane lifetime. Risk: published runs report ozone and PM2.5 so the OH change may already exist in their outputs, and the 1-3% size sits within methyl-chloroform OH uncertainty, and extra NOx-driven chemistry could in rare regimes shift OH the other way, though the sign is unlikely to flip.

title: Lightning-strike soils hold more phosphite and extractable P
untested: Lightning-made phosphite is documented inside one fulgurite, but nobody has measured phosphite, resin-extractable P or ptxD gene abundance in surrounding soil versus matched controls at strike sites in P-poor, lightning-rich regions.

papers.title: Pasek-type study of a Florida fulgurite: lightning reduced apatite-type phosphate to phosphides and a calcium phosphite (CaHPO3); mineralogy only, no soil or microbial release measured
Laboratory fulgurites made from volcanic ash under realistic discharge; reproduced formation conditions, not soil P chemistry or bioavailability
Widespread promiscuous alkaline phosphatases support ancient microbial phosphite oxidation; enzyme evolution, not soil strike sites

web.text: Lightning reducing phosphate to phosphide and phosphite in fulgurites is documented, and microbes widely carry phosphite-oxidation enzymes. Whether this leaves a measurable, bioavailable P signal in the surrounding soil, and in which climates, is untested and likely small and local.

why: Strength: lightning reducing apatite phosphate to phosphides and calcium phosphite is documented in a Florida fulgurite, and phosphite is measurable by 31P NMR and ptxD qPCR. Risk: phosphite oxidizes quickly in soil and the melt is confined to the fulgurite, so the surrounding soil within 1 m may show no +10-50% signal, and fulgurite sampling could even show lower extractable P if melt locks phosphorus into glass.

title: Warm-spell fertilizer ammonia raises downwind cloud condensation nuclei
untested: No study regresses week-to-week satellite NH3 columns (IASI/CrIS) on CCN or droplet number across farm regions controlling for SO2, temperature and humidity, or warms manure experimentally and sizes downwind aerosol to quantify +10-30% droplets per NH3 doubling.

papers.title: Agricultural land in Finland: soil-emitted ammonia and amines with sulfuric acid form new particles that grow to climate-relevant sizes; observed particle formation, not CCN or droplet number across NH3 anomalies
Global impact of anthropogenic NH3 on upper-tropospheric aerosol formation; model and chamber nucleation, not boundary-layer droplet number over farmland
Seabird-colony ammonia drives new particles and cloud-albedo effect in the clean Arctic; natural analogue, clean low-SO2 setting

web.text: Chamber and field work show ammonia greatly boosts sulfuric-acid nucleation, and agricultural ammonia forms new particles in Finland. In polluted farm regions such as the North China Plain, pre-existing aerosol and ammonium nitrate dominate, so a clean +10-30% droplet response per NH3 doubling is untested and may be much weaker.

why: Strength: ammonia boosts sulfuric-acid nucleation by 100-1000 fold in chamber work and agricultural ammonia forms new particles in Finland. Risk: the chain from warm spell to NH3 to nucleation to CCN to droplet number has several uncertain links, and in polluted regions such as the North China Plain pre-existing aerosol and ammonium nitrate dominate, and NH3 covaries with temperature and burning, so nucleated particles may scavenge onto existing aerosol and give no CCN rise.

title: Burned catchments break the atmospheric-river and soil-moisture flood link
untested: No study ranks atmospheric-river landfalls in the first post-fire winters for paired burned and unburned gauged catchments to test burned x AR-rank and burned x soil-moisture interactions, or checks whether the antecedent-moisture correction of the AR scale weakens in burn scars.

papers.title: Antecedent moisture and the AR scale: soil moisture explains divergence between AR rank and peak streamflow across California and Chile catchments; burn status not tested
Upper limits for post-wildfire floods: envelope curve of peak flows (43 m3/s/km2 in small basins); no AR rank or paired unburned control
Eagle Creek Fire debris flows in the Columbia River Gorge: fire raised little long-term erosion relative to background; not AR-ranked and no flood scaling

web.text: It is well established that burned catchments produce much higher peak flows and debris-flow probability, and a 2026 study shows soil moisture explains the AR-rank to flood mismatch in unburned-type catchments. Whether burn scars decouple runoff from antecedent wetness, and by how much at a fixed AR category, has not been quantified.

links.label: Antecedent moisture and AR flood hazard
Fire and debris flows, Columbia Gorge

why: Strength: Burned catchments producing several-fold higher peak flows and debris-flow probability is well established, and gauges, burn-severity maps and AR catalogues exist for the regression. Risk: the weaker soil-moisture correction depends on hydrophobicity that decays within a season and few burned gauged catchments fit the first-winter window, and sediment storage and rainfall intensity could dominate so the interaction flips or vanishes.

title: Fire-spalled granite raises post-fire stream silica and sodium
untested: No paired burned/unburned granitic-catchment study has measured dissolved Si, Na and 87Sr/86Sr after fire with ash subtracted, nor flow-through dissolution of fresh fire-spalled flakes against aged rock surfaces.

papers.title: Fire-induced rock spalling as a weathering mechanism for flared slopes and inselbergs (2019-2020 Australian fires); shows widespread spalling, but no solute or stream chemistry
Fire influence on land-water interactions in aridland catchments: conceptual framework of fire effects on discharge, erosion and water quality; no silicate-weathering flux measured
Post-wildfire water quality in Pacific Northwest: review of monitoring gaps; ash and nutrient pulses, not rock weathering

web.text: Fire spalling of granite is documented and can strip large surface fractions, but I found no stream-chemistry test of whether it raises silica or sodium export. A search summary of an Arctic tundra fire study reported no difference in stream dissolved silica between burned and unburned catchments, attributed to plant uptake, which argues the signal can be small.

why: Strength: fire spalling of granite is documented across the 2019-2020 Australian fires, and Si/Na with 87Sr/86Sr can separate rock from ash in a paired-catchment design. Risk: spalled flakes are a small mass fraction, ash and vegetation uptake dominate dissolved Si (an Arctic fire study saw no silica difference), so a 20% rise may be undetectable, and loss of plant Si uptake or ash Si could mask or reverse the rock signal; it also needs a wildfire at the right place and time.

title: Reservoirs bury rock organic carbon, cutting its CO2 oxidation
untested: No study has cored reservoir sediments in mudrock basins to measure the petrogenic fraction retained, or compared dissolved Re yield per unit erosion between dammed and undammed rivers of similar lithology.

papers.title: Rio Madre de Dios Re budget: over 75% of dissolved Re from rock organic carbon oxidation, with 40% of oxidation in Andean-fed floodplains; no dams or reservoir burial examined
Catchment lithology controls sedimentary OC burial and oxidation in Antarctic Peninsula fjords via ramped pyrolysis; lithology and burial tested, not reservoirs or Re
Persistent organic carbon storage in floodplain deposits over millennia; floodplain OC reactivity, not petrogenic carbon in reservoirs

web.text: Floodplain transit is now shown to double rock organic carbon oxidation downstream of the Andes, so trapping that sediment in a reservoir could plausibly avoid some of that CO2. I found no reservoir-specific petrogenic carbon budget or dam-versus-undammed Re comparison, and most Re-based oxidation occurs upstream in mountains where dams do not intervene.

links.label: Lithology and net carbon balance, Antarctic Peninsula

why: Strength: Re, 14C and Raman methods for petrogenic carbon are mature and burial of trapped mudrock sediment in reservoirs is plausible. Risk: the chain has two uncertain links since most Re-based oxidation occurs upstream of dams, and reservoir drawdown zones can themselves oxidize petrogenic carbon, so the avoided flux of 1-5 Tg C a year could be indistinguishable from zero.

title: Seabird colony ammonia raises downwind cloud condensation nuclei
untested: Colony ammonia driving new particle formation is documented (Arctic and Antarctic), but a paired upwind/downwind CCN spectra measurement against a colony-free coast, and a before/after-breeding-season decline in CCN or droplet number, has not been reported.

papers.title: Croft et al.: seabird-colony guano ammonia drives summer new-particle bursts at Alert; model estimates of cloud-droplet effect and cooling of about -0.5 W/m2; CCN not directly measured against colony-free coast
Penguin guano as a source of Antarctic ammonia and dimethylamine that boosts new particle formation; coastal site observations (preprint), no matched colony-free control or post-breeding comparison
Atmospheric amines review: ppt-level amines boost nucleation and CCN activation; general mechanism not colony-specific

web.text: Arctic and Antarctic work shows seabird or penguin ammonia triggers particle formation and seeds CCN in clean air, with modelled cloud-albedo effects. Direct paired colony-versus-control CCN measurements and the seasonal decline after the colony empties remain to be shown, and the 20-100% range depends on available sulfur and condensation sinks.

why: Strength: Croft et al. 2016 tied seabird guano ammonia to summer new-particle bursts at Alert, with modelled cooling of about -0.5 W/m2, and penguin colonies in Antarctica show the same, so a seasonal on/off test is sharp. Risk: 20-100% CCN enhancement depends on sulfur supply and sea-spray condensation sinks, and a fresh nucleated particle burst may not grow to CCN size, or enhance only small particles, which could leave CCN unchanged despite more particles.

title: Migrating animals deepen oxygen loss and boost ocean nitrogen loss
untested: Migrant respiration is known to deepen oxygen depletion at OMZ upper margins in a global model, but nitrite, N* and denitrification responses, and paired biomass-versus-oxygen/nitrite observations across OMZ margins, have not been tested; the 5-20% nitrogen-loss change is unchecked.

papers.title: Bianchi et al.: ADCP-derived migration depths plus a global model show diel migrators intensify oxygen depletion at OMZ upper margins; BLING model did not resolve denitrification or N loss
California Current budget quantifying sinking particles, vertical migration and physical pump carbon export and sequestration; carbon not nitrogen loss, no OMZ margin model

web.text: Bianchi et al. 2013 showed with a coupled model that migrators concentrate oxygen consumption in poorly ventilated upper waters and deepen suboxic margins of OMZs. Because denitrification and anammox depend sharply on suboxia, an effect on N loss is a natural next step, but no model or observational study I found quantified it.

links.label: Multiple biological pump pathways, California Current

why: Strength: Bianchi 2013 showed migrators intensify oxygen depletion at OMZ upper margins, and denitrification and anammox switch on sharply at suboxia, so N loss should follow. Risk: migrants avoid the anoxic core so their respiration may sit above it, and their organic matter delivery could also fuel denitrification, so removing them might change N loss by less than a few percent; biomass-oxygen covariance is confounded by circulation.

title: Excluding birds and bats cuts seasonal canopy carbon gain
untested: Exclosure experiments show more arthropods and leaf damage, but few if any measure canopy photosynthesis or leaf-area-integrated carbon gain, so the 3-10% carbon loss, and whether compensation erases it, is unmeasured.

papers.title: Japanese temperate forest factorial exclusion: without birds and bats arthropod density rose 81% and herbivory 42%; carbon gain not measured
Subtropical forest bird/bat exclusion with spider removal on Machilus: leaf-chewing damage rose, sap suckers unchanged; no photosynthesis or growth measured
34-year bird exclosure experiments in four prairie systems: top-down control (plants down, grasshoppers up) in only 13% of cases, plants and grasshoppers varied with context

web.text: Recent exclosure experiments confirm that removing birds and bats raises arthropod density and leaf damage by tens of percent in forests. A link from that damage to measurable loss of canopy carbon gain is much less documented, and grassland studies show top-down control is context dependent, so the 3-10% figure is unverified and may be too high given compensatory growth.

links.label: Birds, bats and ants across forest strata
Insectivores and spiders in subtropical forest
How often are ecosystems top-down controlled

why: Strength: exclosures raised arthropod density 81 percent and herbivory 42 percent in a Japanese forest, so lost leaf area should cut canopy carbon gain. Risk: leaf damage is usually a few percent, so the 3-10 percent carbon loss may be hard to detect, and compensatory regrowth, higher photosynthesis of remaining leaves, and context-dependent top-down control (13 percent of prairie cases) could erase or reverse the loss.
